header: Date: 2026-10-30 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 56m | Attendees: Samira P. (Redwood AE), Diego M. (Redwood SE), Elena R. (CTO, Sparrow), Mark O. (Lead ML Eng), Priya S. (PM). Call type: Discovery - model selection + deployment path (hosted/dedicated/private).
transcript_text:
[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick round of intros, then we'll go through what you're trying to solve, constraints, and then Diego will walk through model tradeoffs and deployment paths.
[00:15] Elena (Sparrow CTO): Hi all, Elena here. We're a B2B SaaS for field service optimization, heavy on long-form transcripts and operational documents. key thing: we need reliable summaries and action extraction across long sessions, sometimes entire multi-hour transcripts.
[00:30] Mark (Lead ML Eng): Hey team. to add, we run multilingual support—EN, ES, FR, PT—also some Japanese for APAC. Current infra is GCP, and we use BigQuery, and a self-hosted vector DB. latency target is 100-150ms per token on critical paths, but for batch jobs we can accept higher.
[00:48] Priya (PM): we also care about cost; we've scoped a pilot budget but want clear cost per 1k tokens comparison for hosted vs dedicated.
[01:05] Samira: great, that helps. quick qualification: any regulatory requirements or data residency?
[01:12] Elena: HIPAA-adjacent for a subset of customers, not full PHI yet, but post-contract we may need private deployment or VPC peering. also SSO SAML, audit logs, retention controls.
[01:25] Diego (Redwood SE): Understood. big themes I'll focus on: model selection (open models vs Redwood-verified variants), context length needs, multilingual tokenization nuances, tool-calling for retrieval and DB actions, and deployment options (hosted, Dedicated, Private). we'll also flag the benchmarking plan.
[01:40] Diego: First, on models: you mentioned long sessions — are we talking 32k tokens, 64k, or longer? what does typical session look like?
[01:50] Mark: Average session is ~18k tokens but we have outliers up to 55k when a whole day's notes are uploaded. so ideally support up to 50k, maybe 64k for future-proofing.
[02:03] Diego: okay that pushes us toward models with native long-context or Redwood's KV/cache + sliding window. open-model candidates I recommend testing: Llama-3 (various sizes), Mistral-longformer variants, MPT-30b with extended context, and a few quantized mixes. each has tradeoffs: latency, quality on multilingual, and memory footprint.
[02:22] Elena: how confident are you in multilingual quality from those open models? we need parity with English for summaries and QA.
[02:30] Diego: good q. Llama-3 base variants are strong for many languages but tokenization and pretraining data skew matter. Mistral tends to be strong on instruction following but some smaller Mistral-long variants mis-handle Japanese. MPT sometimes underperforms on non-Latin scripts unless fine-tuned. part of the pilot will be language-specific benchmarks.
[02:50] Priya: any quick wins for language parity without huge cost?
[02:55] Diego: yes — two levers: 1) targeted fine-tuning or instruction tuning on your corpora for the priority languages; 2) using a hybrid routing policy: route EN/ES/FR to a larger, higher-quality model, and low-traffic or background tasks to smaller, cheaper variants. Redwood supports policy-based routing and automatic fallbacks.
[03:15] Mark: we liked the idea of routing. question: how does KV cache and prefix caching work with long documents? if we stream a transcript in chunks, can the runtime keep a persistent KV and avoid recomputing?
[03:28] Diego: yes — Redwood's runtime keeps KV cache and you can pin sessions to keep a warm cache. for very long docs we use a combination of prefix caching and chunked retrieval; also we support automatic chunk re-embedding for your vector DB and tool-calling to fetch relevant context rather than sending the whole transcript. there are edge cases with model compatibility — some quantized variants have tighter KV memory limits.
[03:54] Elena: that sounds promising. on the private vs dedicated question: what's typically the tradeoff for a company our size?
[04:01] Samira: high level: Hosted is fastest to ship and lowest ops, but less control. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and better latency SLOs and data isolation for a single-tenant pool. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control for audits and residency — more ops burden and license/installation steps. given your HIPAA-adjacent need and potential VPC peering, many customers start with Dedicated and then move to Private if they require stronger network isolation.
[04:28] Mark: and cost delta?
[04:30] Samira: Dedicated has a monthly committed cost plus usage smoothing; Private is a larger upfront plus annual support licensing. we'll send a detailed pricing doc, but benchmark runs will help calibrate the exact commit size.
[04:44] Priya: tool-calling — we want the model to call retrieval and then execute DB updates via our connectors. can Redwood handle secure tool ops and secrets?
[04:53] Diego: yes — we support tool calling with function schema, and we integrate with customer-side connectors via the private control plane or through secure webhooks. secrets are handled with KMS integrations and HSM options for Private. audit logs are captured in the Console. sometimes the transcript shows a small gap — like, sorry, the connector has a 2s cold-start — but we can mitigate with warmers and connection pooling.
[05:20] Elena: one concern: tokenization variance — cost estimates differ across models because tokenizers split differently, especially for Japanese. how do we benchmark cost / tokens consistently?
[05:31] Diego: we'll run tokenization pass against your prompt set for each model and normalize per 1k tokens. also we recommend measuring end-to-end cost (including retrieval tokens and tool-calls) — Redwood's reporting breaks down token usage per route and model so you can see the economics.
[05:46] Mark: what's the plan for measuring latency SLOs under concurrency? we have times when many field agents sync and generate summaries concurrently.
[05:54] Diego: for the pilot we'll do a staged load test: ramp to your expected peak concurrency, hold, and then include a spike test. we'll instrument per-token latency and tail latencies (p95/p99). Dedicated gives you more predictable tails because of reserved capacity and burst configs.
[06:12] Priya: any regulatory docs we should see now?
[06:16] Samira: yes we'll attach SOC2 Type II, architecture diagram, and a draft DPA. also a VPC peering checklist if you go Private.
[06:25] Elena: good. two more questions: 1) can we pin a model version per customer? 2) how fast are rollbacks if a model regression is detected?
[06:33] Diego: yes to both. you can pin per-route or per-customer. rollbacks are instant at the API routing layer; the console supports canary and A/B routing too, with automatic fallback to a pinned stable variant if quality drops. we also support eval hooks to run prompt suites automatically after deploys.
[06:50] Mark: what's your recommendation for an initial pilot model?
[06:54] Diego: start with a middle ground: Llama-3 20b variant (quantized) for generalization and multilingual, plus MPT-30b as a cheaper fallback for background tasks. run a small set of 10-15 representative prompts in EN/ES/JP to see gaps. if Japanese quality lags, we can swap in a fine-tuned Mistral-long for those jobs.
[07:13] Elena: timeline — we want a pilot within 2 weeks if possible.
[07:17] Samira: feasible. next steps summary: Samira will send security docs and draft pricing, Diego will share benchmark plan + ask for prompt set, Mark will provide prompt set and concurrency numbers, and we'll schedule the pilot kickoff next Wednesday.
[07:33] Priya: also can you include a short runbook for failure modes and whom to contact?
[07:38] Samira: yes, runbook + escalation contacts will be part of the package.
[07:42] Diego: quick note on metrics: we'll emit token counts, model route, per-token latency, cost breakdown, and quality regressions (via your eval prompts).
[07:52] Elena: perfect. thanks everyone.
[07:55] Samira: thanks all, we'll follow up. bye.
[08:00] <<call ends>>

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-hearings (Mistral sometimes transcribed as 'Mistrill'), some speaker overlaps, and natural fillers. We intentionally kept raw phrasing from the call for accuracy.
